text:
If they swallowed it [within the last hour or so](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6620762/) (slow-release pills leave a few hours more), [activated charcoal](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/i/170920118/activated-charcoal) may help, since it binds to a lot of drugs in the gut before the body can absorb them. It only helps with what binds to it, which leaves out alcohol and lithium among other things, and it can also adsorb medication they need. I'd only give it to somebody who's fully alert and able to swallow, because anybody who is vomiting, sedated, seizing or otherwise unable to protect their airway could breathe it into their lungs (aspiration).

If you're unsure charcoal would be of any value to them, poison control may be useful. They're also who to ask when you can't tell what the substance is or what it does in combination with something else they took, or when there may be a delayed risk (the worst coming hours later). I don't treat calling poison control as a mandatory ritual, though, since how useful they are varies by country and by whoever answers. And what they give you is help deciding, so go on with any first aid while you talk to them.
reader: the friend of someone who swallowed too much of a drug about an hour ago, with activated charcoal in their bag and a phone, deciding what to do next

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
